headline: High-risk default interaction: Open Interpreter can read/write the shared filesystem while caveman uses MCP and file-based project artifacts, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: caveman uses MCP and reads/writes project files like CLAUDE.md, while Open Interpreter can read the filesystem and use clipboard/stdin. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if Open Interpreter exposes attacker-controlled file content back into caveman’s context. The pathway is not proven by direct pair evidence, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter writes attacker-controlled text into a file caveman reads as instructions
IF caveman ingests shared workspace content through MCP without provenance filtering
mitigations: Disable shared workspace access between the agents
Restrict caveman MCP sources to trusted, read-only inputs
Keep Open Interpreter out of directories containing prompt files
Add a manual review step before caveman consumes any file content
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all cross-agent file inputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Open Interpreter can read the entire local filesystem and has broad network egress, while caveman touches session logs, memory files, and project notes. If both run on the same machine, sensitive local data can flow from caveman into Open Interpreter and then out over the network. The default blast radius includes secrets and logs, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents run on the same host with overlapping filesystem access
IF caveman stores secrets or sensitive notes in its project files
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different machines or containers
Remove sensitive files from the shared filesystem path
Disable Open Interpreter network egress for the session
Store caveman logs and memory files in an isolated directory
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Open Interpreter can write the filesystem and modify git state, and caveman supports multiple instances with shared-state implications through files. Concurrent writes to the same workspace or repository can corrupt state or overwrite each other without locking. Because the conflict can affect git history and files by default, high is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git repository or shared directory
IF caveman and Open Interpreter run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate working tree
Pause one agent before the other writes
Avoid letting both modify git state in the same repo
Use a lock file around shared directories
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: caveman can consume files and MCP-fed content, while Open Interpreter can generate and act on filesystem changes and shell commands. If caveman’s output is treated as authoritative by Open Interpreter, errors can cascade into executed commands or commits. The pair lacks a built-in verification boundary in the profiles, so the safer high severity fits.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter uses caveman output as direct input to shell commands or git actions
IF caveman produces unverified facts that Open Interpreter executes
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Force Open Interpreter to summarize caveman output before acting
Disable auto-run mode
Keep caveman outputs in a non-executable notes file
requires-engineering: add verification gates before command execution

E_compliance.rationale: caveman touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md, while Open Interpreter can access the entire local filesystem and may send data to configured model providers. That creates a plausible retention and residency mismatch for sensitive local data, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated-data class or jurisdictional mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is stored in caveman project files
IF Open Interpreter forwards those files to a third-party model provider
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared project files
Review provider retention settings before use
Use local-only model providers for the session
Delete transient logs after the run
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries per agent
